source.title: Quantifying lottery tickets under label noise: accuracy, calibration, and complexity
source.authors: V. Arora; Daniele Irto; Sebastian Goldt; Guido Sanguinetti

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps neural-network size and measures train and test error, using the conventional double-descent setup on new datasets and architectures.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own model-size error curves and tabulated full-model test errors. Its calibration findings and results cited from other work are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps width under symmetric label noise and reports test error for full models, as in Nakkiran et al. Authors: 'We first confirm that fully-connected neural networks exhibit both traditional double descent'. This is a setup step for its pruning study, but the size-sweep results are its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that IMP from full models of very different sizes converges to best pruned models of comparable size and error. That size tracks task difficulty and is similar across architectures. Pruned models are less overconfident: better calibrated on synthetic data, slightly underconfident on real clean-label data, and near-optimally calibrated to noisy-label data. Traditional double descent is reproduced only as the setup; the authors say it is not their focus.
record.recipe_differences: Uses size sweeps and test error as in double-descent studies, with symmetric training-label noise and several synthetic and real datasets; it additionally studies iterative magnitude pruning.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies dataset, architecture, network size, and mixture separation ν; label-noise rates differ by experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: IMP pruning of full models of widely varying size yields sparse double-descent curves whose minima coincide at a similar parameter count. This count scales with task difficulty (XOR about 2× linear; fewer CIFAR classes gives fewer parameters). Best pruned models at the interpolation peak greatly cut test error (e.g. MNIST 3-layer 0.176→0.059).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning-based sparse double descent identifies a task-specific effective parameter count, and pruning removes the interpolation-peak penalty.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2023)
record.problems: Curve values are mainly presented in plots rather than numerically; the tabulated full-model results give individual size points but not uncertainty estimates. Experiments use symmetric label noise, and the authors note other noise types are out of scope.
record.rows_left_out: The tabulated best-pruned test-error and parameter-count entries in Table 1 and Table S2, and additional pruning-curve values in Figures 1, 2, and S2, are not separately extracted: they concern pruning-associated sparse double descent rather than the tested unpruned model-size version. The plotted aggregate pruning curves are discussed under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Clean-label settings are untested; all sweeps use 5–25% symmetric label noise. Exact peak location relative to train-error interpolation is not tabulated. Only figure-level evidence covers the first descent below the smallest tabulated size.
Not tested. Models were trained long enough to avoid the epoch-wise regime.
Not tested. There is no sample-size sweep.
Not tested. Only neural networks are used.
Not tested. The pruning-based 'effective number of parameters' is not used to predict peak location on any axis.
Not tested. Label noise is not varied systematically; the appendix only notes 25% noise was 'needed to consistently observe' the curves on XOR. Tuned regularization and multiple peaks are not tested.
Not tested. The curves are not re-plotted against an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: Treat the table rows as points of one series: individually they are cannot_determine, but jointly they show the peak. For ResNet-6 on MNIST, the largest model (0.057) does not regain the smallest tabulated model's error (0.028). Second descent is thus incomplete in the tested range, though V1 does not require it to go lower. All settings deliberately inject label noise, and XOR needed 25% to show the curve consistently. This hints at noise dependence, but no low-noise results are reported, so V6 is not labelled. The text describes Figure S3 (Fashion-MNIST) as only two model sizes, so it is not a double-descent sweep.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests model-size curves in its specified noisy-label settings, not all architectures or settings.
No epoch-wise test-error sweep; the authors say models were trained long enough not to be in the epoch-wise double-descent regime.
No sweep of training-sample count near the interpolation threshold.
The tested models are neural networks; the study does not test whether the curve generalizes across broader model classes or subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
The effective-parameter measure is based on best pruned models; the study does not test whether one measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Label-noise levels are not systematically varied to test the cause of the peak; multiple peaks and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
The study does not re-express the second descent against an alternative effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Two/three-layer FCNs and ResNet-6 on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, two-layer FCNs on Gaussian mixtures; all with 5–25% symmetric label noise
relationships.reason: The figures show a fall-rise-fall in full-model test error (F1-*, F2-*, S2-2layer, S2-ResNet6). The tabulated series confirm the peak and second fall: MNIST 3-layer 0.105→0.176→0.091; CIFAR 0.143→0.187→0.137; 2-layer 0.081→0.194→0.067; ResNet-6 0.028→0.118→0.057.
relationships.display_finding: Test-error sequences confirmed a peak and renewed decline: MNIST three-layer 0.105→0.176→0.091, CIFAR 0.143→0.187→0.137, two-layer 0.081→0.194→0.067, and ResNet-6 0.028→0.118→0.057.
